column1: # Focus catalogue — what a role instance owns.
# Lines starting with # are ignored. The separator is a literal TAB.
# The key IS the instance suffix, so `--roles research:survey` creates `research-survey`
# and picks up the matching focus automatically. `--focus-for <instance>=@<key>` uses a
# template explicitly, and `--focus-for <instance>="free text"` overrides it entirely.
# A focus should say what this instance OWNS, in a way another instance of the same role
# can read and stay out of. Two instances with vague or overlapping focus do the same
# work twice, which is the main way parallelism is wasted.

column3: Prior work and existing results: what is already established, what has been tried and failed, and what nobody has attempted. Produce a map, not a reading list.
Sources and datasets: acquisition, licensing terms, schema, validation, and provenance. Every dataset gets source, date, licence, and retrieval date recorded before it is used.
Reproduce the baseline methods from their original descriptions. Report what did not reproduce as carefully as what did.
The strongest case AGAINST the current direction: who has argued the opposite, and on what evidence.
Neighbouring fields that have solved a structurally similar problem. Report transferable techniques, not analogies.
Primary-source verification of claims already made in this project. For each: does the source exist, say what we claim, and still hold.
Tools, libraries, and existing implementations that already do part of this. Buy-versus-build evidence, with licences.
The primary hypothesis in AIM.md, and the evidence that would falsify it. Report the falsifier's result whichever way it goes.
Ablations and negative controls: which components actually carry the result, and does it survive removing each one.
Fair comparison against the stated baseline. Tune the baseline as carefully as the method — an untuned baseline is not a comparison.
How stable the result is to seed, split, hyperparameters, and data ordering. A result that moves with the seed is not a result.
Error analysis: where the method fails, on which inputs, and whether the failures share a structure.
Statistical validity: sample size, variance, multiple comparisons, and whether the reported difference is distinguishable from noise.
Hunt for target leakage and train/eval contamination. Assume it is present until the splits are proven clean.
How the result changes with data volume, model size, or input length. Report the trend, not a single point.
Backend, data model, and interfaces. Owns the contracts other components depend on.
Client, presentation, and user-facing behaviour. Owns what the user actually touches.
Data pipeline: ingestion, transformation, storage, and migration. Owns schema compatibility.
Build, packaging, configuration, and dependency management. Owns the repository staying buildable.
Performance: measure first, then optimise what the measurement names. No optimisation without a before-number.
Structural improvement of existing code with no behaviour change. Every commit must be behaviour-preserving and reviewable as such.
Wiring components together and owning the seams between them, including failure behaviour at each seam.
Moving existing data or callers to a new shape, with a rollback that has been tested rather than assumed.
Acceptance criteria in AIM.md, verified one by one. A criterion is met only when a check demonstrates it.
Existing behaviour that must not break. Owns the suite that protects what already worked.
Boundary and malformed input: empty, single, duplicate, oversized, wrong type, wrong order, absent.
Behaviour across component boundaries, including what happens when one side fails or is slow.
Keyboard navigation, focus handling, accessible names, contrast, zoom, and reduced motion.
Input validation, authorisation boundaries, secret handling, and injection surfaces. Report findings; do not exploit beyond proof.
Reproduce reported defects and reduce each to the smallest failing case before anyone attempts a fix.
End-to-end task flows: can a user actually complete the job, and where do they stall.
Loading, empty, partial, error, and offline states. The states that are skipped are the ones users hit.
Information architecture: naming, grouping, and hierarchy. Owns whether things are findable.
Surfacing provenance, confidence, staleness, and what the system does not know.
Interface language: labels, errors, and instructions that say what happened and what to do next.
Continuous integration: what runs on every change, how fast, and how clearly it fails.
Deployment path and rollback. A deploy with an untested rollback is a one-way door.
Logs, metrics, and traces sufficient to diagnose a failure without reproducing it locally.
Environment parity and configuration: dev, staging, and production differing only where intended.
Resource usage and spend, with the largest contributors named and measured.
Reconciling the squads' outputs into one coherent result, and naming the conflicts rather than averaging them.
Guarding AIM.md: what is in, what is explicitly out, and what has quietly crept in.
Model correctness: estimand, units, assumptions, and invariants stated before results are produced.
Seeded reproducibility: identical inputs and seeds must yield identical outputs, verified rather than assumed.
Validation boundary: what the simulation has been shown to predict, and what it has not.
Calibration against observed outcomes, keeping calibration, discrimination, and error separate.
Dependency and dataset licences, attribution obligations, and compatibility with how this project is distributed.
Personal data: what is collected, why, where it goes, how long it is kept, and whether that is minimal.
Public claims against verified evidence. Flag anything stated more strongly than the evidence supports.
Key-shape parity across locales: every key present everywhere, no orphans, no drift.
Consistent domain terminology and its glossary, so one concept has one word per locale.
Text expansion, truncation, and bidirectional layout in the actual interface, not in isolation.
Audience, problem, and benefit, stated so a reader knows whether this is for them.
Every quantitative claim traced to a reproducible source. No number without a run behind it.
Release narrative, changelog, and documentation that matches what actually shipped.
